summary:
South Kalimantan is a province of Indonesia, and a visitor here stands under the national framework that governs the country as a whole. The source inventory records no South Kalimantan-specific provision on gender identity, documents, facilities or enforcement: no provincial criminalisation of trans people, no provincial marker rule of its own, and no documented local divergence from the national position.

Indonesia's revised penal code was passed by the House of Representatives on 6 December 2022, signed by President Joko Widodo and took effect on 2 January 2026. It criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with penalties recorded at up to one year's imprisonment where an immediate family member lodges the complaint, and reported elsewhere at up to two years. The code does not name same-sex relationships, but because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity between same-sex couples falls inside the outside-marital-sex restriction. Reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic, and the United Nations is among the critics citing the code's failure to accommodate protections for LGBT people and domestic partnerships.

Gender identity itself is not criminalised. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run an outreach issuing identification papers (KTP) to transgender Indonesians, and electronic ID cards have been issued to transgender people in nine provinces. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors appear on the documents, and the birth-gender entry is printed unless a court order was already obtained. Indonesia offers no third-gender or X marker, legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Physical risk is rising across the country. A feature published in August 2026 documents growing repression facing Indonesia's transgender community, and reporting ties the surge in vigilante attacks on transgender people to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, and transgender women have been targeted in raids by the Jakarta Social Agency. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women under national morality provisions and, in Aceh's case, provincial religious law that applies to anyone present including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in Aceh in February 2025, following the flogging of two men there in January 2021.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. The national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal in March 2016, websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words have been blocked including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Custody carries a documented lethal risk. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him and that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release, which Indonesian police deny. Transgender identity as waria has long been part of Indonesian culture, but cultural visibility has not produced legal protection.
tangentialFactors:
Provincial practice diverges sharply within Indonesia. Aceh and South Sumatra criminalise same-sex activity on top of national morality provisions, while South Kalimantan has no comparable provincial instrument in the inventory; a visitor moving between provinces therefore faces different exposure, and Aceh's religious-law penalties apply to anyone present rather than to residents alone.

Longstanding cultural visibility of transgender people sits alongside formal legal exclusion. The waria tradition is documented as part of Indonesian life, yet the same period has produced administrative gating of documents, censorship rules and public-order raids, so familiarity with trans visibility locally should not be read as evidence of legal safety.

Official rhetoric and enforcement move together. Reporting in August 2026 attributes the rise in mob attacks directly to statements by officials and to the October 2025 presidential decree placing LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy, a pattern in which political speech precedes physical violence.

International criticism has not altered the domestic framework. The United Nations and other external bodies criticised the 2023 penal code for omitting protections for LGBT people and domestic partnerships, and Amnesty International called the June 2025 villa operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy; the provisions took effect regardless.

outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty for sex outside marriage is reported inconsistently across the sources: the code's own framing is recorded as up to one year where an immediate family member complains, while other reporting gives up to two years' imprisonment. Both figures appear in the inventory and the discrepancy is unresolved here.

No source in the inventory covers enforcement in South Kalimantan specifically. Whether police in the province have conducted raids, made arrests under the outside-marital-sex provision or applied any local regulation is not sourced and remains unresolved.

It is not stated whether South Kalimantan is among the nine provinces where electronic ID cards have been issued to transgender people, so documentation access in this province is unresolved.

The status of the 2025 bill on online content presenting LGBT behaviour, and the scope of the blocks on websites and applications, are drawn from reporting rather than primary legal texts; their current operational effect in this province is unresolved.

Allegations surrounding the August 2022 death in custody are contested by the parties, with the family's account of beating and a payment demand denied by Indonesian police, and no independent adjudication is recorded in the inventory.
